lead: Every real program meets bad input, missing files and code that fails halfway. This unit shows how Python catches an error instead of crashing, how it reads and writes files and folders, how code is split into modules and packages, and how patterns are pulled out of text with regular expressions. After it you can write a script that reads a data file, survives a bad row, and saves a clean report into a folder it creates itself.
about: Unit 5 is about failure and storage. Chapter 5.1 gives the four-part frame, try, except, else and finally, that separates normal work from error work. Chapter 5.2 opens that frame: the built-in exception tree, and how to define and raise your own exception classes. Chapters 5.3 to 5.5 push data to disk: opening, reading, writing and appending text files, the formatted files (CSV, tab-separated) that hold tables of records, and the os and sys calls that create, list and move through directories. Chapter 5.6 turns code into reusable modules and packages. Chapter 5.7 adds regular expressions for pulling patterns out of text. Together they let a student write a script that reads a file, survives a bad record, and stores a result.

chapters.idea: A block of code can declare in advance what to do when a statement inside it fails, and what to do whether it fails or not.
chapters.depth: Full syntax and execution order of try, except, else, finally. except with one named class, with a tuple of classes, with 'as e' to hold the exception object, and a bare except (and why a bare except is risky). Show on a trace table why else exists: code that must run only when no error occurred. Show that finally runs even when the block returns, breaks or calls sys.exit. Nested try inside a function. Reading a traceback line by line: file name, line number, function chain, exception class, message. Some syllabi call the except block the 'exception handler' and the uncaught path the 'default exception handler'. Stay with one function at a time; no user-defined classes here.

figure.title: One try statement, four parts
figure.aria: The try block runs, then the error check sends control to the except block when an exception is raised and to the else block when it is not, and the finally block runs in both cases.

chapters.trap: finally beats return: a return inside try or except is thrown away if finally itself returns. else runs only when no exception was raised, so it is not the same place as the code after the try block. A bare except also swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (syntax, runtime and semantic errors, tracebacks), Unit 2 (functions and return values).
chapters.leave: Defining and raising exception classes to 5.2; file errors as OSError examples to 5.3; Tkinter event handling to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Every error is an object of some exception class, and you can pick a built-in class or write your own and raise it on purpose.
chapters.depth: The built-in tree and the categories syllabi list: arithmetic (ZeroDivisionError, OverflowError), lookup (IndexError, KeyError), type (TypeError, ValueError), name (NameError, UnboundLocalError), OS and input/output (OSError, FileNotFoundError), import (ImportError, ModuleNotFoundError). Show that SystemExit and KeyboardInterrupt sit under BaseException, not under Exception, so 'except Exception' does not catch them. Define a class that inherits Exception, add __init__ and __str__ to carry data, raise it, re-raise inside an except block, and use 'raise ValueError(...) from e'. Show a traceback with the custom name in it. Some syllabi write 'exception objects' for this and group the built-ins as 'built-in exception categories'.

figure.aria: A tree of exception classes: BaseException at the top, Exception below it holding ArithmeticError with ZeroDivisionError, ValueError, TypeError, OSError with FileNotFoundError and LookupError with KeyError and IndexError, and SystemExit and KeyboardInterrupt sitting beside Exception rather than under it.

chapters.trap: A class that does not inherit from Exception is not an exception and raise refuses it. Order matters: 'except Exception' placed before 'except ValueError' catches everything and the ValueError block becomes dead code. 'except Exception' does not catch KeyboardInterrupt.
chapters.leave: Tkinter message boxes that report errors to the user go to Unit 6; Java try-catch-throws and serialization belong to another language.

chapters.idea: A file is a sequence of characters on disk that Python reaches through a file object, and a moving pointer marks where the next read or write happens.
chapters.depth: open(path, mode) with r, w, a and the r+ variant; one line on binary mode 'b'. write() and the number of characters it returns, writelines(). read(), read(n), readline(), readlines() and a for loop straight over the file. tell() and seek() to show the pointer. close() and the with statement. Reading numbers back: the file stores text, so int() or float() is needed and str() on the way in; strip() removes the newline. FileNotFoundError from open. Mention encoding='utf-8' once. This is the 'reading/writing text and numbers from/to a file' wording in some syllabi.

figure.title: File object and pointer
figure.aria: open() creates a file object whose pointer starts at 0, readline() returns the first line and pushes the pointer to position 8, a dashed edge back to readline shows the next call, and close() writes the buffered data to disk.

chapters.example:
Question: write the two lines Anil 78 and Bina 91 into marks.txt, close it, append Chetan 65, then read the first line and report the pointer.
f = open('marks.txt', 'w')
f.write('Anil 78\n')   returns 8
f.write('Bina 91\n')   returns 8
f.close()               file holds 16 characters
f = open('marks.txt', 'a')
f.write('Chetan 65\n')  returns 10, file now 26 characters
f.close()
f = open('marks.txt', 'r')
f.readline()            returns 'Anil 78\n'
f.tell()                returns 8
chapters.trap: Mode 'w' erases an existing file before you write one character, so a wrong mode loses the data. A file left open may never flush its buffer. read() at end of file returns an empty string, not an error, so a loop must test for '' or use a for loop.
chapters.leave: CSV and tab-separated formats to 5.4; listing and creating folders to 5.5; file dialogs in Tkinter to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: CSV and tab-separated files store a table as plain text, one record per line, with fields separated by a delimiter.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it short. csv.reader and csv.writer on a file opened with newline=''; delimiter=',' for CSV and delimiter='\t' for tab-separated; pipe-separated as the same idea. Every field comes back as a string, so int() or float() is needed before arithmetic. Quoting when a field itself holds a comma. csv.DictReader named in one line, one line on json as another formatted file. No pandas here.

figure.title: marks.csv read row by row
figure.aria: A two-row table read from marks.csv: row 1 is the name Anil and the marks field 78, row 2 is Bina and 91, with the marks field of each row picked out and a pointer marking that the field arrives as text.

chapters.example:
Question: marks.csv holds two rows, Anil,78 and Bina,91. Read the file with csv.reader and print the average mark.
import csv
rows = []
with open('marks.csv', newline='') as f:
    for r in csv.reader(f):
        rows.append(int(r[1]))
total = 78 + 91 = 169, count = 2, average = 84.5.
Without int(), r[1] is the string '78', and '78' + '91' gives '7891' before any division.
chapters.trap: Fields are strings, so arithmetric on them silently concatenates instead of adding. A comma inside a field must be quoted, and a file opened without newline='' can produce blank rows on some systems.
chapters.leave: Full tables and column operations to pandas in Unit 6; file copying to 5.5.

chapters.idea: The os module does to folders what open does to files, and sys carries the interpreter's own state such as the command line that started the program.
chapters.depth: os.getcwd, os.chdir, os.listdir, os.mkdir, os.makedirs, os.rmdir, os.remove, os.rename, os.path.join, os.path.exists, os.path.isfile, os.path.isdir, os.path.getsize, os.sep. Relative versus absolute paths, and why os.path.join is portable while a hard-coded backslash is not. sys.argv, sys.path, sys.version, sys.exit, sys.stdout. One paragraph on os.walk for visiting a tree. This is the 'manipulating directories' and 'OS and Sys modules' wording in some syllabi.

figure.aria: A folder tree for project/ holding data/ with the new folder 2024/ and a report.txt inside it, a reports/ folder with summary.txt, and the script os_demo.py that created the folders.

chapters.example:
Question: the script add.py is run as  python add.py 12 30 . Give sys.argv and the printed sum, then create the folder data/2024 and check it.
sys.argv = ['add.py', '12', '30'], so len(sys.argv) is 3.
int(sys.argv[1]) + int(sys.argv[2]) = 12 + 30 = 42.
os.makedirs('data/2024') creates data and data/2024 in one call.
os.path.exists('data/2024') returns True.
os.listdir('data') returns ['2024'].
chapters.trap: sys.argv[0] is the script name, not the first argument, so a sum written from argv[1] onward is off by one if you start at 0. os.mkdir fails when the parent folder is missing and again when the folder already exists; os.makedirs with exist_ok=True avoids both.
chapters.leave: The import search path sys.path is explained in 5.6; file dialogs and file menus in Tkinter to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A module is one .py file imported by name, and a package is a folder of modules with an __init__.py file that Python treats as one importable unit.
chapters.depth: import x, from x import y, import x as y, from x import *. What import actually does: find the file, run it once, bind a name. Search order: sys.modules cache, built-in modules, folders listed in sys.path starting with the script folder. Writing your own module, the if __name__ == '__main__' guard, the __init__.py file that makes a folder a package, dotted import of a submodule, dir() and help() for exploring. Name the standard library modules this unit uses: math, random, os, sys, re. Some syllabi write 'packages and modules in Python' for exactly this.

figure.title: What import does
figure.aria: An import first checks the sys.modules cache and binds the name at once if found, otherwise searches the folders in sys.path, runs the package __init__.py, runs the module file once and binds the dotted name.

chapters.example:
Question: mymath.py holds PI = 3.14159 and def square(n): return n * n. A second file uses it, then uses a package shop/billing.py whose gst(amount) returns amount * 0.18. Give the values.
import mymath            mymath.square(7) = 49
from mymath import PI    PI = 3.14159
import shop.billing      shop.billing.gst(1000) = 1000 * 0.18 = 180.0 rupees
shop/__init__.py is empty and exists only to mark shop/ as a package.
chapters.trap: A file named random.py in the working folder hides the standard random module, because sys.path starts with the script folder. A module's top-level code runs once at the first import and not again, so a counter placed at module level holds its old value on the next import.
chapters.prereq: 5.5 (sys.path), Unit 2 (functions), Unit 4 (classes and modules of code).
chapters.leave: NumPy, pandas and Tkinter packages to Unit 6; decorators and metaclasses to Unit 4; the re module's own patterns to 5.7.

chapters.idea: A regular expression is a small pattern language that describes a set of strings, and the re module tests a string against such a pattern.
chapters.depth: Pattern syntax: literal characters, the dot, character classes [0-9] and [a-z], the shorthands \d \w \s and their capital forms as negation, anchors ^ and $, quantifiers * + ? and {m,n}, greedy versus non-greedy, alternation with |, groups with ( ) and reading them back with group(1). Functions: re.match, re.search, re.findall, re.sub, re.split, re.compile for reuse, and the match object's group(), start() and end(). Raw strings r'...' for every pattern. Stop after one mention of lookahead, backreferences and named groups.

figure.title: Groups in 2024-07-05
figure.aria: The string 2024-07-05 split into single characters, with positions 0 to 3 forming group 1, positions 5 and 6 forming group 2 and positions 8 and 9 forming group 3, and the two dashes left unmarked between the groups.

chapters.example:
Question: match the pattern r'(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})' against the string 2024-07-05 and give every group, then find all numbers in Anil 78, Bina 91.
m = re.match(r'(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})', '2024-07-05')
m.group(1) = '2024', m.group(2) = '07', m.group(3) = '05', m.group(0) = '2024-07-05'.
re.findall(r'\d+', 'Anil 78, Bina 91') returns ['78', '91'].
re.sub(r'\d+', '#', 'Anil 78, Bina 91') returns 'Anil #, Bina #'.
chapters.trap: re.match looks only at position 0, so it fails on a date that starts later in the line; re.search scans the whole string. A pattern written in a normal string needs a double backslash, so use r'\d' and not '\d'. Greedy .* eats up to the last possible match, not the first.
chapters.prereq: 5.3 (reading lines from a file), Unit 3 (string methods, slicing).
chapters.leave: Full text parsing tools and tokenizers are out of scope; pandas string columns go to Unit 6.

links: an except block names an exception class, so the class tree comes next
a wrong file name raises FileNotFoundError inside the try block
a CSV file is a text file read line by line
reports written to a file need a folder to sit in
os and sys are built-in modules, so import rules explain them
regex scans the lines that a file gives you
re is a standard library module imported like any other
